story_text.value:
I kept entering coding instruction in the shell by mistake, so I built this shell plugin to intercept the command not found error and pass the prompt to coding agent instead. Now I can type in plain English such as "work on the next task in PLAN.md", and it opens claude code in that directory.

It makes sure regular commands such as `git status` still run as usual. When the shell can't find a command, llmao first checks for likely typos before treating it as a prompt. So it'll suggest git if the command is gti status. It works with zsh, bash, and Fish.

story_text.value:
Offline password manager for Android: a fork of Passdroid (last release 2012), brought up to date. The app has no internet permission.

Two key new features: - 2FA codes (TOTP) - fingerprint unlock

Plus many smaller changes and fixes, and security hardening: AES-256 with PBKDF2 at 600k iterations, AES-GCM encrypted exports. Threat model and design are in INTERNALS.md.

Built largely with Claude Code; the design and security decisions are mine.

Feedback welcome, especially on the security side.

story_text.value:
What if your agents could create (almost) any SQLite database they need?

I built databasedmcp to let Claude (or any other agent) create databases for my sessions, in both Claude and Claude Code.

With the MCP, agents can create multiple databases with basically any schema.

Docs and tool descriptions: https://databasedmcp.com/docs

Some use cases that I've discovered:

* Share data between agents

Let agents store their status, what they're working on, etc. This is essentially about passing data between coding agents.

E.g. set up a worker agent that picks up work items that other agents add to the database. This kind of enables autonomous work discovery.

* Build custom apps

I've built many ad-hoc apps just by describing the idea to Claude. Ask it to create the UI as an artifact and to use databasedmcp as the backend.

Artifacts can call MCP tools however they want. You use the chat to modify the app, and use the app itself in the artifact UI.

Pretty easy to build small apps such as a shopping list, an expense tracker, etc. Then use Claude to extract data from documents, and store the data with databasedmcp in a structured manner.

Any comments are appreciated, thanks!

story_text.value:
I built Klistra: describe your video idea and add your logo, photos or other assets, Klistra designs and animates a video for you, exported for every screen size, with fonts, media and logos kept exact. Deterministic renders make features exact and isolated, allowing for superior control and iteration compared to diffusion models. Here's a short demo render where I made an ad for Klistra itself: https://app.klistra.ai/s/4EQoWCe37SkYz5nThgegzw

As a solo dev with a lot of projects going on, I found myself needing to make short promos or explainer videos. Not being familiar with animation software, I had the idea to use Claude to code up those videos and export them as video files. In the process of creating these clips I stumbled into a bunch of bugs and setup needed to make it work reliably. The list of features I wanted for better control and feedback kept growing and I needed to sign up for a bunch of services to get music, voiceovers and other media into my project. I couldn't find an existing service that had everything I wanted. Seeing these hurdles and that the technology was only easily accessible to people already confident with coding agents, I started working on Klistra, and a couple of months later I'm turning it into a service so you all can use it too.

The goal with Klistra was to include everything I missed in the manual workflow in an easy-to-use service with a nice UI, so people could focus on what they wanted the video to look like, not setting up the framework behind it. Klistra includes precise timeline control, media generation, built-in support to make animations match the rhythm of the background music, word extraction from voiceovers or songs, a dedicated iteration / feedback tool, website import and much more.

Something I knew I needed to get right was making it easy to iterate on small features of the video with precise control of what was being built. I designed Klistra so you first create a specification where you define scenes in detail, describe what you want shown and when, reference media or timestamps in-line, freely drag the timeline around and preview the result before letting a builder agent create the video. If you want to change something, the specification changes and the builder agent gets a diff of what changed. There is also a planner agent built into Klistra that helps create and edit the specification for you (which is what I use the most), while letting you turn to manual fine-tuning when needed.

Don't think of this as a replacement for diffusion models, if you want photorealistic images or videos they clearly do a better job. Klistra really shines when you need motion design and precise control, exact text with your fonts, media such as logos or voiceovers, animated UI that matches your apps and so on. Klistra does have built-in integrations for generating media from diffusion models, and combining the two technologies usually gets the best results.

Everything that costs money to run on Klistra, from machines to AI tokens, is paid for with credits included in a subscription or bought via one-time packs (Pro starts at $25/mo ($20 billed yearly) and packs at $12). Being a solo dev without funding, the budget wouldn't allow for a free tier with enough monthly credits for a real project. I instead decided to give the first 200 of you who sign up 350 free credits, enough for a simple video (the advanced tutorial used around 250 credits).

There is also a Claude Code integration in paid subscriptions, where your agent can act as a planner, convenient if you already have a project built with Claude that has all the context and you need an explainer, ad or social post. It also reduces credit spending if you're a heavy planner user.

- Tutorial, mostly using the planner: https://klistra.ai/docs/basic

- Advanced features and manual control: https://klistra.ai/docs/advanced

- More demos: https://klistra.ai/

Happy to hear what you think!

story_text.value:
I’m writing my first novel and could not find an app that fit my workflow: quiet like iA Writer, organized like Scrivener, and with AI so I can discuss my book while I write it. It allows me to feel less “alone” and have a sounding board while I write.

- A book is a folder of plain Markdown files. Musset commits to a git repo, tracks versions and drafts without you having to know git.

- Revisions are CriticMarkup inside the text. It manages docx revisions too, so your editor can edit a Word doc and you import their comments.

- PDFs are typeset using Typst, embedded in the app, following each language’s typographic rules.

- Spelling and grammar are checked using LanguageTool, also embedded.

- Mac/Word, WordStar, vi and Emacs keyboard modes.

The AI is optional and uses your Codex or Claude Code CLI. It comments, leaves margin notes, and checks continuity and your chapters against your style rules.

It’s GPL-3.0 and free during the beta. When or if it reaches 1.0, if there is sufficient interest, the idea is to make it a small one-time payment ($9.90). There is a paid sync service (git hosting) that lets you share a book with beta readers and editors.

Download: https://musset.app

I’d love to have some feedback!

story_text.value:
Hi Hackernews! I just wanted to share a game I've made over a few weeks just as a little side project. Of course it was developed using Agents Engineering. The idea of the game though comes from around 10 years ago, from conversations with my brother: he is an artist and back them he was experimenting with chromatic paintings that looked differently depending on which color of light they were exposed to. A few weeks ago I decided to show my brother what's possible now a days with AI and how we can turn ideas into reality with a fraction of the effort we would have need in the past. The game is a little platformer, meant to be challenging but cute and entertaining, taking inspiration of games like Celeste or Meatboy. Death is part of the game, and light mechanics are introduced over the course of the 63 levels that are available to play.

The development was made fully from my phone with Claude Code, but I invested lots of time on play testing it and I've involved several friends to play it to gather feedback and improve it.

I'd love to hear your feedback and I hope some of you have fun playing it!

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I’m Bryant, founder of ArkViz (https://arkviz.io). ArkViz is a product to automatically generate architecture diagrams from your codebase using AI.

The vision behind ArkViz is to supercharge both AI agents and humans by providing AI agents deeper relational context using structured model diagram formats, and by providing humans with a rich visual representation you can interact with, with features like zooming, panning, search, and show composing files.

In this new age of AI, you can generate a structured model diagram from your codebase in seconds, quicker and better than a human. Not only can the generated diagram be a visual documentation tool for humans, AI agents can also benefit from the context of a pre-generated architecture diagram that lives alongside a project’s codebase. This concept has already been proven by context files like CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, ARCHITECTURE.md living in the root of your repository.

The differentiator between ARCHITECTURE.md and ArkViz is that ArkViz generates a structured model diagram of the system, while ARCHITECTURE.md is broader in scope and purely text. ArkViz aims to be a supplement to ARCHITECTURE.md to provide deeper understanding like how components are connected, which components live inside other components, which files compose a component.

—

Why ArkViz?

Software engineering teams often create diagrams to aid in the documentation of their software systems. They are incredibly useful for onboarding new engineers and understanding projects. However, they take time to create and maintain, so are often non-existent or out of date. ArkViz automates the creation and maintenance of software architecture diagrams, seamlessly and securely.

AI agents thrive when they have high quality context, including for architecture diagrams. However not all diagram formats out there are optimized for AI. A diagram showing connected systems and components can be represented in essentially 3 ways:

1. Unstructured drawing / canvas format (e.g. draw.io, Excalidraw, Figma, LucidChart)

  - Quick to get started but hard to maintain.
  - Good for brainstorming and whiteboarding
  - The format carries no semantic meaning and is basically represented by pixels, shapes, and vectors. Positioning is stored
  - Passing this to an AI agent as context has questionable value.
2. Structured diagramming formats (e.g. Mermaid, d2lang)

  - A level of abstraction higher than a 2D drawing canvas
  - Good for quick isolated diagram, like on GitHub
  - Represented by nodes and edges, nested hierarchies. Layout is generated
  - Better for AI agents, although they have to piece together the context, and might get confused by an inconsistency like duplicate naming
3. Structured modeling formats (e.g. Structurizr, LikeC4, IcePanel).

  - These have an underlying data model and single source of truth
  - High quality documentation, but hard to create and maintain
  - Represented by entities and relationships. Layout can be richer, like zooming into a component and seeing what's inside
  - Best for AI agents, since they have a single source of truth context
ArkViz currently uses LikeC4 for its diagram format, a modern, popular, and open-source architecture-as-code format that supports interactive diagrams. AI agents will be more trained with this than a proprietary format.

Why not roll my own solution with something like Claude Code? While Claude Code is a powerful AI coding harness, ArkViz provides seamless features you'd rather not spend time building like hosting diagrams, access control, scheduling automation, handling errors and retries, logs, connectors to GitHub. Additionally, ArkViz has battle-tested, optimized multi-pass prompts, validators, and guardrails for the specific purpose of AI generated architecture diagrams.

Take a look here: https://arkviz.io! Feedback greatly appreciated on which features you care about, and whether you think the value proposition is there.

story_text.value:
Hello!

One of my hobbies is curling in a league with the local curling club. From time to time, there's a setup of stones that is tricky and interesting to contemplate from a strategic perspective. A while back, I started working on a three.js-based curling simulator that would enable me to recreate situations from my league games and then try different shots.

As you may know, curling is notoriously tricky from a physics perspective. There are a variety of papers out there about this, including this one, which is one of the more recent dives into understanding why stones curl the way they do: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-26595-y

Anyhow, with the help of Claude Code, I pulled together the work and converted the quick-and-dirty sim into a game you can play online. It's still a bit more of a sim than a game, perhaps, but it can be fun to play as a game.

Curling often is referred to as "chess on ice" because there's more strategy in choosing shots and playing ends than there would appear to be at first glance. The primary challenge of turning this into a game has been trying to figure out how to provide the computer player both with a policy for game and end-level strategy while also having it evaluate the tactical choices that have to be made for each shot.

For example, when would the computer try to blank (no points scored) an end deliberately so that it can retain hammer (last stone thrown) in the subsequent end? When should it throw a low vs. high center or corner guard in an attempt to make up a point deficit? When should it try to steal points from the hammer team vs. throwing protective stones that hold the hammer team to one point?

It's a fun side project for me, so I thought you all might enjoy giving it a shot. :)

p.s. In a game, if you go into the settings, you can turn on debug mode, which will reveal a panel on the right with a variety of (currently-undocumented) parameters you can tweak.

title.value: Show HN: Online curling game/SIM with Three.js

For example, when would the computer try to blank (no points scored) an end deliberately so that it can retain hammer (last stone thrown) in the subsequent end? When should it throw a low vs. high center or corner guard in an attempt to make up a point deficit? When should it try to steal points from the hammer team vs. throwing protective stones that hold the hammer team to one point?

It's a fun side project for me, so I thought you all might enjoy giving it a shot. :)

p.s. In a game, if you go into the settings, you can turn on debug mode, which will reveal a panel on the right with a variety of (currently-undocumented) parameters you can tweak.
